stemMd:
Two of the three sides of a triangle have lengths $5$ and $9$.

| Quantity A | Quantity B |
| --- | --- |
| The perimeter of the triangle | $20$ |
instructionsMd: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B and select the one statement that is true for every value consistent with the information given.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

explanationMd:
Nothing fixes the third side, so the right move is to find the full range it can occupy and see whether the comparison survives across that range.

**Step 1 — bound the third side.** Call it $s$. The triangle inequality says each side must be shorter than the sum of the other two and longer than their difference:

$$9 - 5 < s < 9 + 5, \qquad \text{that is} \qquad 4 < s < 14.$$

**Step 2 — turn that into a bound on the perimeter.** The perimeter is $P = 5 + 9 + s = 14 + s$, so adding $14$ throughout gives

$$18 < P < 28.$$

**Step 3 — test the comparison.** The threshold $20$ lies strictly inside that interval, so both outcomes are reachable. Take $s = 5$: the sides $5, 5, 9$ form a genuine triangle and $P = 19 < 20$. Take $s = 11$: the sides $5, 9, 11$ also form a genuine triangle and $P = 25 > 20$. Two admissible triangles give opposite answers, so **the relationship cannot be determined**, choice (D).

**How to check.** Verify that each example really is a triangle before you trust it. For $5, 5, 9$: $5 + 5 = 10 > 9$. For $5, 9, 11$: $5 + 9 = 14 > 11$. Both pass. The general discipline on Quantitative Comparison is to hunt for two legal cases that disagree; if you find them, you are finished, and if the quantity is genuinely pinned down you will fail to find them.

distractorRationale.a: Chosen by assuming the third side must be the longest, or at least large, so that the perimeter comfortably exceeds $20$. Nothing forces that: $s$ may be as small as just over $4$, which puts the perimeter just over $18$.
distractorRationale.b: Chosen by assuming the third side must be the shortest, giving a perimeter below $20$. The third side can be anything up to just under $14$, so the perimeter can reach almost $28$.
distractorRationale.c: Chosen by picking one convenient third side, often $6$, computing a perimeter of $20$ and stopping there. A single consistent case only shows that one value is possible; equality has to hold for every admissible triangle before (C) is correct.

accessibilityText: Two of the three sides of a triangle have lengths 5 and 9; the third side is not given. Quantity A is the perimeter of the triangle. Quantity B is the number 20. Decide which quantity is greater, whether they are equal, or whether the relationship cannot be determined.

provenance.notes: Original item written for the wave 3 top-up. The threshold 20 was chosen deliberately to sit strictly inside the interval of possible perimeters, so the triangle inequality alone decides the item. Not adapted from any ETS question.

review.author: gre-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Triangle inequality puts the third side strictly between 4 and 14, so the perimeter lies strictly between 18 and 28. A third side of 4.5 gives perimeter 18.5 (< 20) while 9 gives 23 (> 20), so the relationship changes.

review.notes: Author derived 4 < s < 14 from the triangle inequality, hence 18 < P < 28. Counterexamples 5, 5, 9 (P = 19) and 5, 9, 11 (P = 25) straddle 20, so the answer is D. Awaiting blind independent solve.
